interventions.title: Make food the plan
interventions.whyLine: This is hunger. Hunger needs food, not a willpower exercise.
steps: Pick a meal or a filling snack you can get right now.
If it is easy, add more than one thing, like carbs plus protein or fat.
Eat enough to settle the hunger. Do not chase one exact taste.
Come back only if another check-in would help. Do not skip or make up for this food later.
swaps: Toast with eggs, cheese, or nut or seed butter

interventions.title: Eat a steady snack
interventions.whyLine: A snack now is easier than an emergency later, when your appetite comes back all at once.
steps: Pick one easy source of energy you will actually eat.
Add something that lasts if you have it, like protein, fat or fiber.
Eat enough to meet the need. HabitWise does not tell you portions.
Once you have eaten, rate the craving again. It may not need following.
swaps: Fruit and nut or seed butter
A snack plate with familiar foods

interventions.title: Eat before the dip hits
interventions.whyLine: You said hunger rises as your medication wears off. That is a sign to plan food, not to fight your appetite.
steps: Treat the hunger as real and pick a balanced meal or snack that is easy to get.
Choose something that needs few decisions.
After you eat, check the craving again instead of just following it.
If your appetite changes a lot, or in a way you did not expect, talk to your prescriber. HabitWise will not suggest dose or timing changes.

interventions.title: Use your personal safety plan
interventions.whyLine: Possible glucose warning signs need your established medical plan, not a craving exercise.
steps: Stop this flow.
Follow the glucose plan provided by your care team, if you have one.
Seek urgent help for severe symptoms, loss of consciousness, seizure, or if you cannot keep yourself safe.

interventions.title: Choose nourishment and support
interventions.whyLine: When restriction or compensation is present, delay and resistance tools can reinforce the wrong pattern.
steps: Skip the timer and choose nourishment.
Contact a trusted support person or care professional if you can.
Use emergency or crisis support if you may be in immediate danger.

interventions.title: Check if this is hunger
interventions.whyLine: A few minutes away from the cue tells you whether you are hungry or whether one food is calling.
steps: Step away from the food, the delivery app, or whatever started this.
Ask yourself: would several normal meals sound good right now, or only this one thing?
Take seven easy minutes. Sit somewhere quiet, walk a bit, or drink water if you are thirsty.
Rate the urge again. If you are clearly hungry, eat a proper meal or a balanced snack.
swaps: Choose a balanced meal only if genuine hunger is present

interventions.title: Rest first, then decide
interventions.whyLine: When you are tired your brain grabs the fastest reward it knows. That is not the same as needing this food.
steps: Leave the food cue and turn down one thing: light, noise or a task.
Close your eyes and breathe out slowly five times.
Move gently for a minute, or sit somewhere comfortable.
Rate the urge again. If you are hungry, eat a proper meal or a balanced snack instead of grabbing this.
swaps: A balanced meal if genuine hunger is present

interventions.title: Deal with thirst first
interventions.whyLine: A dry mouth can look like a food craving. Clear it and the real urge is easier to read.
steps: Move away from the food cue.
Drink a few comfortable sips of something suitable.
Wait five minutes doing something else away from food.
Rate the urge again and check for hunger. Water is not a meal. If you are hungry, eat.
swaps: A non-food activity in another room

interventions.title: Check the appetite, not just the craving
interventions.whyLine: Your appetite may genuinely be up right now. That does not mean this one food is the answer.
steps: Step away from this specific food for seven minutes.
Ask whether lots of foods sound good. That points to real hunger.
Drop one demand and do something comforting that is not food.
Rate the urge again. If you are hungry, eat a balanced meal or snack. If symptoms are severe or getting in the way, get clinical support.
swaps: A heating pad if normally safe for you
A balanced meal if genuine hunger is present

interventions.title: Take the pressure down
interventions.whyLine: Calming your body a little gives you room to choose. The feeling does not have to go away first.
steps: Leave the food, the kitchen or the ordering screen for seven minutes.
Sit with your back or feet supported and breathe out slowly five times.
Name the one pressure that feels loudest, then shrink it to a single next action.
Do that action, then rate the craving again before any food decision.

interventions.title: Comfort yourself without the food
interventions.whyLine: Comfort can come from somewhere else. Otherwise your brain learns that every hard feeling ends in this food.
steps: Get the food out of sight and name the feeling in a word or two.
Pick one physical comfort: warmth, something soft, pressure, quiet or movement.
Stay with it for ten minutes with food apps and cues closed.
Rate the urge again and name one thing that would help the feeling itself.

interventions.title: Ground yourself and wait it out
interventions.whyLine: When your attention is racing, naming what is around you brings it back to now.
steps: Step away from the food cue and find three things you can see.
Notice two places where your body touches something.
Find one sound close by and one further away.
Keep going for five minutes, then rate the urge before you go back.

interventions.title: Give yourself a different win
interventions.whyLine: When your mood or energy is flat, one small action can be its own reward.
steps: Leave the food cue and pick something you can start in under a minute.
Make it noticeable: brighter light, one loud song, cold water on your face, or quick movement.
Keep at it for seven minutes without opening food apps or going back.
Rate the urge again and pick one more non-food action if it is still loud.

interventions.title: Reach out instead
interventions.whyLine: Some of what you want from the food is contact with someone. Ask for that directly.
steps: Move away from the food cue and pick the easiest person or place.
Send a short message, a photo or an emoji. It does not have to turn into a conversation.
If nobody is free, go where other people are, or play a familiar voice.
Stay with it for ten minutes, then rate the urge before you go back.

interventions.title: Take one thing off your plate
interventions.whyLine: When everything is piling up, less load helps more than more willpower.
steps: Leave the food cue and list what is pulling at you.
Pick exactly one and drop it, hand it off, push it later, or make it smaller.
Work on the smallest next step for seven minutes.
Rate the craving again. If you turn out to be hungry, eat properly instead of using food as an escape.

interventions.title: Choosing it on purpose
interventions.whyLine: This is for a decision you make on purpose, not the default answer to a craving.
steps: Check that you did both plans and looked again for real hunger or a medical need.
Say why you are choosing this food and whether the choice still fits what you want.
If it feels impulsive, go back to getting distance and support instead.
If you do choose it, log it without shame. Do not skip food later or write off the rest of the day.
swaps: Leave the cue until the urge falls
Make a deliberate decision only after the review

interventions.title: Pick the reward you actually want
interventions.whyLine: Name what you are after and you can usually find a better match than food.
steps: Leave the food cue and ask what you want: rest, fun, credit, company, or an end to the day.
Pick one non-food reward that matches it.
Give it your full attention for ten minutes.
Rate the craving again and note whether what you wanted changed.

interventions.title: Cut off the cue
interventions.whyLine: If the thing that started this stays in front of you, it keeps restarting the urge.
steps: Name the cue: something you saw, a route, a smell, a place, a notification, an open packet.
Close it, cover it, put it away, or walk out now.
Spend ten minutes somewhere else with your hands busy.
Rate the craving before you go back. Do not reopen the cue to test yourself.
swaps: Put the package out of sight

interventions.title: Stop it before it becomes autopilot
interventions.whyLine: Noticing the cue and acting on it are two different things. This puts a gap between them.
steps: Say what the cue was in one sentence and move away from it.
Ask whether you are hungry or whether you only want this one item.
Do something non-food that takes your hands or attention for seven minutes.
Rate the urge again and stay away from the cue if it is dropping.
swaps: Return to what you were doing

interventions.title: Break the screen and snack habit
interventions.whyLine: Screen and food have been running together. Change how it starts and you get a choice back.
steps: Pause the screen and step away from the food for a minute.
Check whether you are hungry or whether the urge started with the screen.
Start the screen again with something in your hands: a fidget, a craft, notes.
Keep going for ten minutes, then rate the craving without opening food content.

interventions.title: Make the other option the easy one
interventions.whyLine: Wanting the easy thing is not weakness. So make something else easy.
steps: Close the food cue or the ordering screen.
Pick the easiest non-food action that changes where you are, what you are looking at, or how awake you feel.
Take away one setup step so you can start right now.
Keep going for seven minutes, then rate it. If you are hungry, eat a proper balanced meal rather than following the cue.

interventions.title: Swap what comes next
interventions.whyLine: Your brain expects something after the cue. Give it something else.
steps: Name the cue and what you expect to get from the old routine.
Keep the same moment, but put a different action where the food used to go.
Repeat the new action for ten minutes without checking the food.
Rate the urge again and note whether the new action gave you any of what you expected.
swaps: Same time with a short walk
Same route with one new stop

interventions.title: Build a better switch-off
interventions.whyLine: The old routine was how you switched off. Give yourself a clearer way to do that.
steps: Say what just ended and what is next, then leave the food cue.
Change one thing you can feel: clothes, light, music, temperature or room.
Give yourself ten minutes with nothing demanded of you and no food content.
Rate the urge again. If you are also genuinely hungry, switch to the meal plan.

interventions.title: Start the task, then decide
interventions.whyLine: Not knowing where to start is what makes escaping feel urgent. Starting shrinks it.
steps: Close the food cue and name the first visible step of the task.
Do that step now, even if it is only opening the file or finding one thing.
Keep going for ten minutes, or until one small piece is done.
Rate the craving before you take a break, and make the break a non-food one if the urge is still about this item.

interventions.title: Match the feeling, not the food
interventions.whyLine: Name what you actually want, crunch or cold or warmth, and you can try it another way first.
steps: Move away from the food and name the main thing you want: crunch, cold, warm, creamy, spicy, chewy or strong flavor.
Pick a safe non-food version of it using touch, sound, temperature, movement or smell.
Use it for seven minutes without checking the food.
Rate the urge again, and check for hunger separately.
swaps: Use gum only if it is safe for you

interventions.title: Give your mouth something else
interventions.whyLine: Sometimes the want is chewing, sipping, cold or strong flavor, not food.
steps: Move away from the food and check whether lots of foods sound good. If they do, use the hunger route.
If this is mostly about your mouth, pick a safe non-food mouth activity.
Use it for seven minutes, and only if it is safe for your teeth, swallowing, allergies and sensory needs.
Rate the craving again and switch to movement or touch if it is still strong.

interventions.title: Give your brain something louder
interventions.whyLine: A bored brain takes food as the nearest interesting thing. Offer it something more interesting.
steps: Leave the food cue and pick one channel: movement, sound, touch or something to look at.
Pick something strong enough to hold you but safe and easy to stop.
Use it for ten minutes without checking the food or the delivery app.
Rate the urge again and try a different channel if the first did not fit.
swaps: A change of lighting or location
